newsitem.title: USA: US stocks end lower, thumped by Greenspan comments.
newsitem.headline: US stocks end lower, thumped by Greenspan comments.

text.p: Wall Street stocks stumbled on Wednesday, hit by a new round of warnings from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that sent U.S. financial markets reeling.

Greenspan, delivering his semi-annual report on the U.S. economy to the Senate, spoke in surprisingly blunt terms of his concerns about the risks of inflation as well as the dramatic increase in stock prices.
The Dow industrials fell 55 points to 6983. The S&P 500 index and Nasdaq Composite also finished lower.

Greenspan, whose passing rhetorical reference to "irrational exuberance" during a December speech sent global financial markets reeling, left little question he remained concerned about the market's advance and urged caution.
"Such caution seems especially warranted with regard to the sharp rise in equity prices during the last two years," he said. "These gains have obviously raised questions of sustainability."
He also said inflation remains "quiescent" but warned the Fed might have to raise interest rates in anticipation of a pickup in inflation.
The testimony sent a jolt through the bond market, triggering a sell-off that saw yields on the 30-year U.S. Treasury shoot up to 6.78 percent from 6.65 percent yesterday.

The heavy selling quickly spilled over to stocks and sent the Dow tumbling more than 120 points before a late session recovery. Despite the partial rebound, analysts said Greenspan appeared to have accomplished his goal of talking down the market.
"It looks like Greenspan did a better job of jawboning the market this time," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"I think he's got the bond market clearly thinking the Fed's going to raise rates instead of doing nothing and that's taken the steam out of this market," he added.
With many analysts already warning that the stock market was due for a pause, several said any further advances were almost certainly on hold for now.
"I do think his remarks may, on top of the strong performance we've seen this year, serve to be something of a constraint on the upside," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.
The interest rate sensitive financial and transportation sectors were especially hard hit as a result of the bond market's decline.
Among financials, BankAmerica Corp fell 2-1/2 to 119-3/8, Merrill Lynch and Co Inc fell 2-1/8 to 95-3/4 and Chase Manhattan Corp dipped 2-1/2 to 103-1/4.
Southwest Airlines Co slipped 7/8 to 23-7/8 and United Airlines parent company UAL Corp fell 1-3/8 to 59-1/8.
Among individual issues, McDonald's Corp dropped 2-5/8 to 44-5/8. The company confirmed it was considering chain-wide reductions in the prices of various sandwiches.

Fears that the discounting could trigger a price war also cut into shares of fast-food franchise competitors like Wendy's International Inc, which fell 1-1/2 to 20-3/4. U.S.-listed shares in U.K.-based Burger King parent Grand Metropolitan Plc shed one point to 30-5/8.
Petrolite Corp jumped 10-3/8 to 58-3/8 after agreeing to be acquired by Baker Hughes Corp.
Shares in Baker Hughes, which will pay $61 in stock for each Petrolite share, ended unchanged at 35-1/2.

Dell Computer Corp rose 3-5/8 to 75-3/4 in the first trading after the company reported stronger than expected earnings. Other direct marketing personal computer companies were also strong, including Gateway 2000 Inc, which gained 3-3/8 to 64-5/8.
The good news failed to prevent today's sell-off from afflicting other tech shares, however, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 7.14 points to 1340.55.
The S&P 500 index fell 6.35 points to 805.68.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
